source: SEP Positions on the Epistemology of Disagreement (peer disagreement, equal weight)
finding: Defines the three theses of conciliationism: Defeat, Equal Weight, Independence. Splitting the difference moves the attitude, not the content.
numbers: Credence example: peers at 0.7 and 0.3 should both move to 0.5. Restaurant check: you get $43 each, friend gets $45; you should end near equal credence in both.
limits: Entry read to character 100,000 of 137,396. Attribution of the restaurant case to Christensen 2007 is from the entry.
agent_relevance: Core frame for G4. A second sample is a peer only if its reliability can be judged without looking at the disputed answer.
quote: Reasons to discount your peer must be independent of the disagreement itself.

source: SEP Positions on Disagreement: steadfast views (Kelly, Lackey, right reasons)
finding: Steadfast replies: Uniqueness Thesis and permissivism, right-reasons view, justificationist view (Lackey), total evidence view (Kelly). Each denies Defeat, Equal Weight or Independence.
numbers: Kelly bootstrapping case: both misjudge evidence at 0.3 and land on 0.7 and 0.9, then converge on 0.8. Lackey cases: Elementary Math (2+2=4), Lucky Lotto.
limits: Philosophical argument, no measured data. True peers are rare in practice.
agent_relevance: Right-reasons view says a correct agent need not move. A strong verifier could outrank samples, but only if it is truly independent of them.
quote: Uniqueness Thesis: for any body of evidence E and proposition P, E justifies at most one competitor doxastic attitude toward P.

source: SEP Positions on Disagreement: formal issues, many dissenters, self-defeat
finding: Equal weight has formal problems: Gardiner and Wilson argue it violates commutativity of evidence, so the order of meeting peers changes the result. With many dissenters only right-reasons avoids skepticism; agreement among people with shared background counts for less.
numbers: No numeric data. Self-defeat: conciliationism must apply to itself (Bogardus, Elga, Pittard responses).
limits: Summaries of debates, not tests.
agent_relevance: Matches G4: N agreeing samples from one model count as roughly one opinion. Order of aggregation can change the outcome, so aggregate once, not sequentially.

source: Elga (2007) Reflection and Disagreement, Nous 41(3) 478-502
finding: Proposes the equal weight view: after learning an advisor disagrees, your probability that you are right should equal your prior conditional probability that you would be right.
numbers: Reductio: if you were 70% confident you are right in each disagreement over a long series of races, you would end up very confident you are the better judge, which is absurd.
limits: Elga uses a non-standard peer definition: equally likely to be mistaken conditional on disagreement. Prior is taken before thinking through the issue. Philosophical, no data.
agent_relevance: The pre-disagreement prior is the key idea: decide how much to trust a second opinion before seeing the answer. A scaffold can fix voter weights up front.
quote: your probability that you are right should equal your prior conditional probability that you would be right

source: Elga (2007) section 8: many peers and the unwelcome consequence
finding: With many peers on a tricky issue, equal weight makes your view depend on the fraction of peers who agree, so you must suspend judgment on many controversial matters. Elga notes the assumption that peers reached views independently.
numbers: Footnote 15: the generalization holds if one judges that one's peers reached their conclusions independently. Footnote 16 links to the free-rider problem (List and Pettit 2003).
limits: Philosophical. Independence is an explicit assumption.
agent_relevance: Direct statement that counting heads is valid only under independence. G4 is this assumption applied to LLM samples.

source: Elga (2007) section 9: extra weight and right-reasons competitors
finding: Extra weight view: give your own assessment somewhat more weight, so you move less than half way. Right-reasons view: if your assessment is in fact right, you may stay put. Elga says equal weight denies both: even if correct you should not favor yourself a tiny bit.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Argument.
agent_relevance: An agent cannot know whether it is the one who is right, so self-preference gives no principled tiebreaker. Use external checks.

source: Elga (2007) end sections: clean cases versus messy real-world cases
finding: Elga resolves the spinelessness worry: in clean cases you can count someone a peer by reasoning independent of the disputed issue. In messy real-world cases your reasoning about the issue is tangled with other beliefs, so you rarely count dissenters as peers.
numbers: No numbers. Cites Christensen 2004: explanations of a disagreement must be evaluated independently of the disputed issue.
limits: Argument, not an experiment.
agent_relevance: A reliability estimate for a sample must come from something other than its answer on this item, for example track record on checkable items.

source: SEP Epistemology of Testimony: reductionism versus anti-reductionism
finding: Reductionism (Hume, Fricker) needs positive reasons to trust a speaker. Anti-reductionism (Reid, Coady, Burge, Goldman 1999) gives a defeasible default right to believe if there is no undefeated defeater.
numbers: Objections: global reductionism faces circularity and regress (Coady 1992); local reductionism fails for 3-year-olds and for stranger directions; humans are poor at detecting unreliable testimony.
limits: Read to character 100,000 of 117,618. Goldman's veritism was not in the portion read.
agent_relevance: Choice for an agent reading text from other models: default trust with defeater checks, or demand evidence per source. G4 argues for the latter when sources share errors.

source: Lackey (2008) cases as reported in SEP testimony entry
finding: Creationist Teacher: Stella teaches evolution she does not believe; students come to know it, which challenges the view that testimony only transmits knowledge. Alien notebook case suggests anti-reductionism permits gullibility.
numbers: Thought-experiment cases only; no counts.
limits: Thought experiments, contested.
agent_relevance: A summary step can pass on correct claims it does not itself endorse; but gullible acceptance of unvetted text is the risk. Keep defeater checks.

source: SEP Social Epistemology: Goldman veritism and the Condorcet Jury Theorem
finding: Goldman (1999) Knowledge in a Social World judges social practices by how reliably they produce true beliefs. Condorcet (1785): if each member is more than 50% likely correct and judges independently, majority accuracy rises toward 1 as the group grows.
numbers: Theorem needs two conditions: competence above 0.5 and independence. Bikhchandani et al. (1992) information cascades show how copying earlier choices hides private information.
limits: Read to character 100,000 of 114,294. Goldman's expert-selection criteria were not found in the portion read.
agent_relevance: The theorem is the formal basis for self-consistency voting. When samples share errors the independence premise fails, so more samples need not raise accuracy (G4).

source: Network epistemology as summarized in SEP: Bala-Goyal, Zollman effect, Hong-Page
finding: Zollman (2007, 2010): in Bala-Goyal style models, more densely connected communities are generically worse, because misleading early evidence spreads and locks in a poor theory. Hong and Page (2004): diverse random groups can beat groups of top performers.
numbers: No numbers in the text read. Mayo-Wilson, Zollman and Danks (2011): rational groups can be built from irrational individuals and the reverse.
limits: Secondary source only; the Zollman paper itself was not opened (publisher returned 403). Hong-Page has later critiques not covered here.
agent_relevance: Supports limited information sharing between parallel reasoning threads: keep samples isolated until aggregation to preserve transient diversity.

source: Du, Li, Torralba, Tenenbaum, Mordatch (2023) Improving Factuality and Reasoning in Language Models through Multiagent Debate
finding: Several instances of a model propose answers, read each other's, and revise over rounds. Debate beat single agent, reflection and majority vote on arithmetic, GSM8K, biographies, MMLU and chess.
numbers: Table 1 (3 agents, 2 rounds): Arithmetic 67.0 single, 69.0 majority, 81.8 debate. GSM8K 77.0, 81.0, 85.0. Chess pawn score 91.4, 102.2, 122.9. Table 2: biographies 66.0 to 73.8; MMLU 63.9 to 71.1.
limits: Mostly one model family (chatGPT) and small samples (GSM8K 100 problems).
agent_relevance: Positive result for debate, the baseline other papers dispute. Debate beats majority vote here, but later work finds this does not hold across settings.
quote: the population almost always converges on a single and more accurate common answer

source: Du et al. (2023) side findings: cross-model debate and personas
finding: Mixing chatGPT and Bard on 20 GSM8K problems: Bard solved 11, chatGPT 14, joint debate 17. Different persona agents on MMLU lifted accuracy from 71.1 to 74.2.
numbers: Cases exist where all agents start wrong and debate reaches the right answer (their Figures 4 and 11).
limits: Tiny sample (20 problems) for the cross-model test; persona gain is one run.
agent_relevance: Different model families may supply the independence same-model samples lack, but the evidence here is thin.

source: Du et al. (2023) debate and uncertain facts (biographies)
finding: Under debate, instances disagree on uncertain facts and drop them from the answer, so fewer false facts appear in biographies.
numbers: Biographies: 66.0 single agent, 68.3 reflection, 73.8 debate.
limits: Disagreement serves as an uncertainty signal only if instances are not strongly correlated (see Kim et al.).
agent_relevance: Disagreement across samples is a useful hint of uncertainty. Agreement is not proof (G4).

source: Smit et al. (2023/2024) Should we be going MAD? Multi-agent debate strategies for LLMs
finding: Benchmarks several multi-agent debate protocols against self-consistency and ensembling. Debate in its current form does not reliably outperform other prompting strategies.
numbers: With hyperparameter tuning some MAD systems (Multi-Persona) do better; adjusting agent agreement levels can lift debate above all non-debate protocols tested. Per-dataset numbers not extracted.
limits: Only the abstract and introduction were read; tables were not extracted.
agent_relevance: Debate costs more calls and is fragile to settings. A cheap independent-sample vote is the safer default.

source: Wynn, Satija, Hadfield (2025) Talk Isn't Always Cheap: failure modes in multi-agent debate
finding: Debate among GPT-4o-mini, Llama-3.1-8B and Mistral-7B can lower accuracy compared with majority vote over initial answers, even when stronger models outnumber weaker ones. Accuracy often falls round by round.
numbers: Setup: 3 agents, 2 debate rounds, 100 random questions per task, 5 seeds; CommonsenseQA, MMLU, GSM8K. On CommonsenseQA debate always harmed. Correct-to-incorrect flips outnumber incorrect-to-correct flips.
limits: Small models, small samples. Table cell values did not extract; only directions are recorded here.
agent_relevance: LLM analog of conciliation going wrong: models give peers too much weight. Do not let a sample revise on seeing another sample's answer.
quote: models frequently shift from correct to incorrect answers in response to peer reasoning, favoring agreement over challenging flawed reasoning

source: Wynn et al. (2025) social influence and the correctness-payoff test
finding: The chance a correct answer flips to incorrect depends on how many other agents agree with it. A prompt giving payoff only for correctness did not reduce harmful flips and sometimes increased them.
numbers: Agents that resisted in round 1 resisted less in round 2. Variation across models and datasets was large; on GSM8K, GPT and Mistral flipped less than Llama.
limits: Figures 4 and 5 read as text; no per-cell numbers extracted. Payoff idea borrowed from political science bonus studies (Bullock et al. 2015, Prior et al. 2015).
agent_relevance: Telling a model to value truth over agreement is not enough. Structure (isolation, ordering) must do the work, not an instruction.

source: Yao, Shang, Du, et al. (2025) Peacemaker or Troublemaker: How Sycophancy Shapes Multi-Agent Debate
finding: Defines a Disagreement Collapse Rate (DCR) and a Sycophancy Score. Debate does not consistently beat single-agent baselines, especially decentralized debate. Sycophancy makes disagreement collapse before a correct conclusion.
numbers: Table 1, CommonsenseQA, 2 agents Qwen-Qwen: single 85.50, decentralized 83.62 (DCR 81.71%), centralized judge 86.65 (DCR 41.27%). Llama-Llama decentralized 83.70 (DCR 86.36%). MMLU Pro 3-agent Qwen decentralized 72.10 vs single 66.46.
limits: Qwen3-32B and Llama3.3-70B only. A judge reduces collapse but needs its own independence.
agent_relevance: Disagreement is valuable only while kept. Reading another sample's answer tends to end it. Supports isolating samples and using a separate judge.

source: Yao et al. (2025) persona control of sycophancy
finding: Low-sycophancy personas (troublemaker) helped; high-sycophancy (peacemaker) hurt. Effects are larger in mixed-model debates.
numbers: Homogeneous Qwen-Qwen, 45 persona settings: accuracy 81.98% to 83.87%, lowest with both peacemakers. Heterogeneous Qwen3-32B and Llama3-70B, 81 persona settings: 78.95% to 82.06%, peak with both troublemakers.
limits: Ranges are small (about 2 to 3 points). One dataset in this analysis (CommonsenseQA).
agent_relevance: G4 forbids persona voters on single-answer problems; this paper shows persona gains are small. Consistent with the guardrail.

source: Kim, Garg, Peng, Garg (2025) Correlated Errors in Large Language Models
finding: Over 350 LLMs, errors are strongly correlated. When two models are both wrong they agree on the wrong answer far more than chance. Larger, more accurate models are more correlated, even across providers.
numbers: Helm: pairs agree about 60% when both wrong, random baseline 1/3; 97.5% of pairs above baseline. HuggingFace: mean 0.423 vs random 0.127; 100% of pairs above. Features explain 34% to 62% of variation. Llama-3.2-90B vs Llama-3.1-70B: 0.97. Models: 349, 71, 20 across three datasets.
limits: Resume task uses subjective human labels as truth. Agreement metric conditions on both being wrong.
agent_relevance: Strongest evidence for G4. Voting among strong models does not give independent evidence; agreement on a wrong answer is the common case.
quote: models agree 60% of the time when both are wrong

source: Kim et al. (2025) correlated errors: sources and LLM-as-judge
finding: Same developer, same base architecture and similar size each raise error agreement. A judge model systematically inflates accuracy of models from its own provider or architecture, and under-rates models more accurate than itself.
numbers: HuggingFace regression: same-architecture coefficient 0.398 as read from the table text. Hiring simulation: more monoculture raised the systemic exclusion rate.
limits: Regression table text extraction was garbled; only the architecture coefficient and the direction of other effects were read reliably.
agent_relevance: A judge from the same model as the solver is not an independent peer. Use another family or checkable ground truth for verification.

source: Panickssery, Bowman, Feng (2024) LLM Evaluators Recognize and Favor Their Own Generations
finding: LLM evaluators score their own outputs higher. Self-preference rises in step with self-recognition. GPT-4 tells itself from two other LLMs and humans with 73.5% accuracy out of the box.
numbers: All three models (GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Llama 2) beat 50% self-recognition untuned. After fine-tuning on 500 examples, GPT-3.5 and Llama 2 exceed 90%. Self-preference strength is linearly correlated with self-recognition. Tasks: XSUM and CNN/DailyMail.
limits: Summarization only. Causal link shown by fine-tuning, not natural variation.
agent_relevance: Self-review by the same model is a biased peer. Pair with an external check or a different model for judging.

source: Sharma et al. (2023) Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models
finding: Five AI assistants frequently wrongly admit mistakes when questioned, give biased feedback, and mimic user errors. Human preference data and preference models sometimes reward sycophantic answers.
numbers: Claude 1.3 wrongly admits mistakes on 98% of questions in the are-you-sure test. A user suggesting an incorrect answer can reduce accuracy by up to 27% (LLaMA 2).
limits: Concerns user challenge, not a peer model. 2023 model versions.
agent_relevance: Challenge from any apparent peer pushes a model off a right answer. Do not use 'are you sure' as a repair step without new evidence.

source: Schoenegger, Tuminauskaite, Park, Tetlock (2024) Wisdom of the Silicon Crowd
finding: A crowd of 12 LLMs forecasting 31 binary questions matched 925 human forecasters in a three-month tournament and beat the no-information benchmark.
numbers: Study 1: LLM crowd Brier M=0.20 (SD=0.12), human crowd M=0.19 (SD=0.19), t(60)=0.19, p=0.850; equivalent under Cohen d=0.5 bounds (0.081 Brier). Study 2: seeing the human median improved GPT-4 and Claude 2 by 17% to 28%, but less than averaging human and machine forecasts.
limits: Acquiescence bias: mean model forecasts well above 50% though outcomes nearly even. Equivalence test not preregistered. Only 31 questions.
agent_relevance: A crowd of different model families can match human crowds. Averaging beat letting a model read the crowd, which fits keeping samples isolated.

source: SEP disagreement: actual versus possible disagreement, deep disagreement
finding: Christensen's reply: actual disagreement shows someone erred, raising the chance of error; merely possible disagreement only reaffirms known fallibility. Disputes over what counts as evidence may block treating someone as a peer.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Argument summary.
agent_relevance: Actual disagreement between samples is evidence of error on this item; absence of disagreement among correlated samples is not evidence of truth.

source: SEP disagreement: higher-order evidence and Titelbaum Fixed Point Thesis
finding: Right reasons view treats peer opinion as higher-order evidence; your competence and the peer's cancel, leaving the first-order evidence you responded to correctly. Titelbaum: mistakes about rationality are rational mistakes.
numbers: No numbers. Remaining problem: its verdict in the restaurant check case seems wrong to many.
limits: Contested.
agent_relevance: Re-derive from first-order evidence (tests, calculation) when available, rather than weigh opinions.
